passages.title: Online Learning Is Here to Stay
text: When schools around the world closed during the COVID-19 pandemic, online learning was treated as an emergency measure, something to be abandoned as soon as classrooms reopened. Yet several years later, digital platforms remain part of everyday education. Far from being a temporary fix, online learning has become a permanent and valuable part of how we learn.

The first argument is access. A student in a remote village can now watch lectures from top universities, join coding courses, or practise English with learners on other continents. For people who cannot leave their jobs or families to attend classes, online programmes offer a chance to gain qualifications that would otherwise be out of reach.

Second, online learning allows students to learn at their own pace. Recorded lessons can be paused, replayed, and reviewed before an exam, which is especially helpful for students who need more time to understand difficult concepts. Adaptive platforms can even adjust the difficulty of exercises based on each student's answers, providing a level of personal attention that a single teacher with forty students cannot.

Third, digital skills are now essential in almost every career. Students who regularly use online tools learn to manage files, communicate in virtual teams, and find reliable information on the internet. These are precisely the skills that employers increasingly demand.

Critics are right that online learning has weaknesses: it depends on stable internet connections, and it cannot fully replace the social experience of school. However, these problems are arguments for improving and combining online learning with face-to-face teaching, not for abandoning it. Blended learning, which mixes both, offers the best of both worlds. Online learning is not the enemy of the classroom; it is its most powerful extension.

passages.title: Renewable Energy Is Indonesia's Best Option
text: Indonesia's demand for electricity is growing rapidly as its economy expands and its population increases. For decades, most of this electricity has come from coal. Continuing on this path, however, would be a serious mistake. Indonesia should invest heavily in renewable energy, for both economic and environmental reasons.

To begin with, Indonesia is exceptionally rich in renewable resources. As a tropical country on the equator, it receives strong sunlight throughout the year. It also sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, which gives it some of the largest geothermal reserves in the world. Its many rivers offer hydropower potential, and its long coastlines could support wind and ocean energy. It would be wasteful not to use these advantages.

In addition, renewable energy is becoming cheaper. Over the past decade, the global cost of solar panels has fallen dramatically, and in many countries new solar and wind farms now produce electricity more cheaply than new coal plants. Once built, renewable plants need no fuel, so they protect the country from sudden rises in coal and oil prices.

Most importantly, burning coal harms both health and the climate. Coal plants release fine particles that cause breathing problems, and they are one of the largest sources of the greenhouse gases that drive climate change. As an archipelago with millions of people living in low-lying coastal areas, Indonesia is particularly vulnerable to rising sea levels.

It is true that the transition requires large investment and that solar and wind power depend on weather conditions. Nevertheless, improvements in battery storage and a mix of different renewable sources can provide a stable supply. Indonesia has the resources, and the technology is ready. What is needed now is the political will to make renewable energy the backbone of the nation's power system.

passages.title: Repairing, Not Replacing
text: A cracked screen or a weak battery is often enough to make people throw away a smartphone that is only two or three years old. In many cases, the phone could easily have been repaired, but repairs are made difficult by the manufacturers themselves. Consumers should have the right to repair the devices they own, and manufacturers should be required to make repair possible.

Many modern devices are designed in ways that discourage repair. Batteries are glued in place, special screws require tools that ordinary people cannot buy, and spare parts are available only to authorized service centres, which often charge high prices. Some companies even use software that shows warning messages when a part has been replaced by an independent technician.

This situation is costly for consumers. When a repair costs almost as much as a new device, people have little choice but to buy a replacement. Making spare parts and repair manuals available to everyone would create competition among repair shops and bring prices down. It would also support small businesses, such as the thousands of phone repair stalls found in markets across Indonesia.

The environmental argument is even stronger. Electronic waste is one of the fastest-growing types of waste in the world, and only a small share of it is properly recycled. Discarded devices contain toxic metals such as lead and mercury that can pollute soil and water. Extending the life of each device by even one or two years would significantly reduce the amount of e-waste produced.

Manufacturers argue that independent repairs may be unsafe or may damage their products. Yet the European Union has already introduced rules requiring that certain devices be easier to repair, showing that such regulations are practical. If a product belongs to us, we should be free to fix it.

passages.title: Indonesia Must Protect Its Mangrove Forests
text: Indonesia is home to about one-fifth of the world's mangrove forests, yet every year large areas are cleared for fish ponds, housing, and industry. This trend must be stopped because mangroves provide protection, food, and climate benefits that are very costly to replace.

First, mangroves protect coastal communities. Their thick roots slow down waves and hold the soil in place, so villages are less likely to suffer from erosion and flooding. After storms, communities behind healthy mangroves usually suffer less damage than those living along bare coastlines. Building concrete sea walls to do the same job costs far more, and these walls need constant repair.

Second, mangroves support the fishing industry. The roots provide shelter for young fish, shrimp, and crabs. Many of the species that fishermen catch offshore spend the early part of their lives in mangrove waters. When the forest disappears, the catch of local fishermen often falls, which means less food and less income.

Third, mangroves help to fight climate change. They absorb carbon dioxide and store large amounts of carbon in their roots and in the mud beneath them. Scientists have found that, per hectare, mangrove soils can store more carbon than many forests on land. When mangroves are cut down, much of this stored carbon is released back into the air.

Some people argue that turning mangroves into shrimp farms brings quick profits. However, these profits are often short-lived, because the ponds lose productivity within a few years and are then abandoned, leaving damaged land behind. In conclusion, Indonesia should protect its remaining mangroves and restore the damaged ones for the sake of coastal safety, local livelihoods, and the climate.
